title: Sing, Barren Woman: The Covenant of Peace
summary: Zion, pictured as a barren and abandoned wife, is told to sing and enlarge her tent because her children will be more than she can hold. Her Maker is her husband, and though he forsook her for a brief moment in anger, he will take her back with everlasting compassion and swears, as he did after Noah's flood, that his covenant of peace will not be broken. The chapter ends with a vision of a city built of precious stones, whose children are taught by the LORD and whom no weapon can overcome.
story: Chapter 53 ended with the Servant seeing his offspring and dividing the spoils after bearing the sin of many. Chapter 54 shows what that looks like: a desolate woman suddenly surrounded by children. The movement from the Servant's suffering to Zion's joy is deliberate. The individual Servant disappears from view, and from here on Isaiah speaks instead of the servants of the LORD (verse 17), the people who inherit what his suffering won. The marriage imagery also resolves the question raised in 50:1 about whether God had divorced his people.
historical: For the exiles and for those who returned to a depopulated Judah in the late sixth century BC, the image of a barren, widowed woman described their situation with painful accuracy. Jerusalem had been emptied by death and deportation after 587 or 586 BC, and the first groups who came back after Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC were small. Ezra 2 lists the returning families, and the total given (Ezra 2:64) is modest for a people once counted as a kingdom. The promise that her descendants will spread to right and left and inhabit desolate cities spoke to people rebuilding amid ruins. The reference to Noah in verse 9 reaches back to the covenant God made after the flood (Genesis 9:8-17), the oldest promise in Scripture that God will restrain his judgment.
cultural:
In ancient Israel a woman's security and standing depended heavily on her husband and her children. Barrenness was experienced as a deep grief and often a social shame (as with Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah), and a widow with no sons had no one to protect her or carry on the family name. The chapter uses every part of that vulnerability: barren, deserted, widowed, rejected. Then it reverses each one.

The tent imagery of verse 2 recalls Israel's nomadic ancestors. Enlarging a tent meant adding curtains, lengthening the ropes, and driving the stakes deeper to hold a larger structure, something a family did when it grew. The jeweled city of verses 11 and 12 uses building language. The word translated “antimony” was a dark mineral used as eye paint (Jezebel painted her eyes with it in 2 Kings 9:30); here it becomes the mortar for gemstones, an image of lavish, almost playful beauty. The exact identity of some of the stones is uncertain, as with many ancient gem names.
literary: The chapter is a poem of promise in two main parts. Verses 1 to 10 use the image of the wife: first as barren woman (1-3), then as deserted wife taken back (4-8), capped by God's oath like the oath to Noah (9-10). Verses 11 to 17 switch to the image of the city: its foundations, walls, children, and security. The contrasts in verses 7 and 8 are carefully balanced: a brief moment against great compassion, a surge of anger against everlasting kindness. The word “servants” in verse 17 is the first plural use of the term in this part of Isaiah, and it becomes the regular way the remaining chapters (56 to 66) speak of God's faithful people.

outline.t: Sing, barren woman: enlarge your tent
Your Maker is your husband: the deserted wife called back
An oath like Noah's: the covenant of peace
A city of jewels whose children are taught by the LORD
No weapon formed against you: the heritage of the LORD's servants

doctrines.note: God calls his promise a “covenant of peace” and binds it with an oath like the one after the flood (verses 9 and 10). Covenant here is not a contract between equals but God's sworn commitment that his loving devotion will outlast the mountains.

The chapter pictures God's relation to his people through marriage: “your husband is your Maker” (verse 5). It also honors the grief of barrenness and widowhood rather than dismissing it, and it pictures the fruitfulness God gives as abundant family.

The chapter never pretends the past was not painful. It calls the anger real and the abandonment real, but brief, and places it inside everlasting compassion. Hope here is grounded in God's character, not in improved circumstances.

words.note: Chesed, loyal love, covenant kindness, what the BSB often renders “loving devotion.” It describes love that keeps faith with a commitment even when the other party has failed. In verse 8 God contrasts a surge of anger with “everlasting kindness,” and in verse 10 he says his chesed will not depart though the mountains move.

Baal, to marry or to be a husband, from a root meaning to own or be master. The same letters form the name of the Canaanite god Baal, whom Israel had so often worshiped. In verse 5 God claims the role of husband for himself: Zion's true husband is her Maker, not the gods she ran after.

Limmud, taught, a disciple. “All your sons will be taught by the LORD” (verse 13) uses the same word that described the Servant in 50:4, who was taught morning by morning. What the Servant was, his children will become. Jesus quotes this promise in John 6:45.

christ: Paul quotes verse 1 in Galatians 4:27, applying the barren woman's many children to the church of Jews and Gentiles, born by promise rather than by natural descent, as Isaac was. Jesus quotes verse 13 in John 6:45 to say that everyone who has listened to the Father comes to him. The New Testament also develops the chapter's marriage imagery: Christ loves the church as a husband (Ephesians 5:25-27), and Revelation 21 pictures the new Jerusalem as a bride, with foundations of precious stones (Revelation 21:2, 19-21), echoing verses 11 and 12. These links follow the direction Isaiah set: after the Servant's suffering comes a people, and the New Testament identifies that people as those who belong to Christ.

hard.q: Did God really forsake his people and hide his face in anger?
hard.a: Verses 7 and 8 say so plainly, and many readers find it hard that God would speak of abandoning anyone. The text does not soften it. The exile was experienced as real abandonment, and Scripture lets God own it rather than blaming Babylon or chance. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some stress that the language is relational and covenantal: God withdrew his protective presence as the covenant curses had warned (Deuteronomy 31:17), a real judgment on real sin. Others stress the proportion the text insists on: a brief moment against everlasting compassion. Christian readers often connect this with the cry of Psalm 22:1 on Jesus's lips, in which the experience of forsakenness is taken up by the one who bore sin. On any reading, the chapter treats the forsaking as temporary and the compassion as permanent.

questions: The barren woman is told to enlarge her tent before any children arrive. What would it look like to prepare for God's promises before you see them?
How does the image of God as husband in verses 5 to 8 challenge or comfort you, especially if your own experience of marriage or family has been painful?
Verse 17 says vindication comes from God. Why is that harder to trust than defending ourselves against every accusing tongue?
